title: The Mystery of the Sleepy Sickness
summary: A medical mystery episode on encephalitis lethargica (sleepy sickness), an epidemic illness that emerged around 1916 and spread across several continents by 1919, killing hundreds of thousands. The hosts cover its acute and chronic forms, the symptoms (hypersomnolence, ophthalmoplegia, mania, akinesia, waxy flexibility, post-encephalitic parkinsonism), early research by Constantin von Economo and Renée Cruchet, theories about causes (toxins, Spanish flu, streptococcus, herpes, autoimmune disorder), and the later 1960s patients described in Oliver Sacks' book Awakenings and its film adaptation, including L-dopa treatment. The episode also includes banter and two listener mails, one about the Buffalo radio "kart" and another correcting a band name.

entities.name: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening and introduction to encephalitis lethargica
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the medical mystery of encephalitis lethargica, also called the sleepy sickness, and describe the early 20th-century outbreak and its unknown origins.

segments.title: Origins: von Economo and Cruchet
segments.summary: The outbreak began around 1916 in Europe. Constantin von Economo at the University of Vienna and French physician Renée Cruchet described the illness; Economo argued it was an infectious epidemic.

segments.title: Symptoms and the nature of the sleep
segments.summary: Early cases resembled flu. The hallmark hypersomnolence was not restful sleep; patients could be woken easily and might freeze mid-action.

segments.title: Case examples and neuropsychiatric effects
segments.summary: Deaths often occurred within days or weeks; one girl died after paralysis on her way home from a concert. Some survivors developed behavioral changes such as kleptomania.

segments.title: Acute forms: somnolent, ophthalmoplegic, hyperkinetic
segments.summary: Economo grouped acute cases into three forms: the most deadly somnolent-ophthalmoplegic form, the hyperkinetic form with mania and sleep reversal, and the least common hypokinetic akinetic form.

segments.title: Akinetic form and waxy flexibility
segments.summary: In the akinetic form patients become statue-like and can be posed, a state called waxy flexibility. Brief discussion of a bizarre case report and of the name waxy flexibility.

segments.title: Consciousness trapped inside frozen patients and chronic form
segments.summary: Patients were often fully conscious but unable to respond. The chronic form could appear years after an acute case, producing post-encephalitic parkinsonism that differs from Parkinson's disease.

segments.title: Chronic symptoms and naming of post-encephalitic parkinsonism
segments.summary: Chronic cases added mood swings, psychosis, and puns; the defining trait was the statue-like state, called post-encephalitic parkinsonism.

segments.title: Awakenings book and film connection
segments.summary: The hosts reveal that the chronic patients were the subject of Oliver Sacks' book Awakenings, which was adapted into the film with Robert De Niro; Sacks worked with about eighty patients at Beth Abraham Hospital in the Bronx in 1966.

segments.title: Film details and paradoxical kinesia
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1985 NPR interview with Sacks, the film's director and cast, and how Sacks identified patients by tossing a ball, showing paradoxical kinesia.

segments.title: Disappearance of the disease and unanswered questions
segments.summary: The epidemic lasted roughly ten years and vanished; about nine thousand papers were written but key questions, such as contagiousness, remained open given mixed anecdotal evidence.

segments.title: Ruling out toxins and defining encephalitis
segments.summary: The hosts define encephalitis as brain and spinal cord swelling and explain that toxic causes were quickly ruled out.

segments.title: Infection theories: influenza and Spanish flu
segments.summary: Infectious encephalitis was considered, and early flu-like symptoms suggested influenza. Genome testing of Spanish flu RNA in brain tissue showed it was not the cause.

segments.title: Strep theory, Mathieson Commission, and other ideas
segments.summary: Streptococcal infection was studied, including Economo's 1931 dog experiment. The Mathieson Commission, funded by a businessman, issued reports that ended with suggesting herpes as a possibility. Tangential talk about a tabloid headline and a band-name correction.

segments.title: L-dopa treatment and its effects
segments.summary: L-dopa, developed in the late 1960s for Parkinson's, temporarily revived the Awakenings patients, though many later developed side effects and relapsed.

segments.title: Patient experiences and tangents on the film
segments.summary: One patient, Rose, described feeling disconnected from time since 1926. Hosts discuss the film's sad ending and the book's postscripts noting some patients improved.

segments.title: Triggers for movement and modern understanding
segments.summary: Music, touch, and sirens could prompt movement; a cobbler patient worked at a bench on L-dopa. Modern theory suggests an autoimmune reaction triggered by infection, targeting brain proteins. Only about eighty case reports in seventy-five years.

segments.title: Closing banter
segments.summary: Brief wrap-up of uncertainty about the disease, with lighthearted banter about movie impressions.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Buffalo kart
segments.summary: A listener from Buffalo explains that radio personality Iron Mike Benson used a loop tape cartridge, or kart, to play sound effects over songs, connecting to a prior episode on the term kart.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite email; show credit given.
